Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-22
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 69 minutes
Attendees: Alex Nguyen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Miguel Torres (Sierra Infra), Dana Li (Sierra Sec), Ravi Patel (Sierra MLOps)
Recording id: ff-record-20250422-7b3c

Auto-generated summary (may be noisy): Redwood walked through offline artifact delivery, license activation in air-gapped environments, GPU driver version mismatches we've seen, and KV cache warm-start best practices. Agreed on next steps and action items.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Alex Nguyen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'll hand off to Priya in a sec — Priya's going to run through the install/artifact flow and the driver compatibility matrix we've seen with on-prem installs.
[00:24] Priya Shah: Yeah hi, thanks Alex. Quick context — this call is focused on Sierra's air-gapped rollout and the peculiarities: offline licensing, artifact transfer (we'll talk tarball vs iso), and GPU driver requirements. I'll be somewhat SE-heavy so feel free to jump in with infra questions.
[00:50] Miguel Torres: Thanks. Our main ask is: we have an upcoming pilot on 30th May, but due to change freeze windows we need a reproducible offline install that security signs off on. We also run a mix of A100 40GB and 80GB nodes, some older V100s.
[01:12] Dana Li: And from security: we need signed artifacts, SHA256 verification, and we cannot allow any outbound phone-home. HSM for key material is our preference.
[01:30] Priya Shah: Absolutely. The high-level artifacts we'll provide: redwood-agent-2.1.tgz, runtime-image-2025.04.tar.gz, and an optional precompiled quantization pack for common models (q4_0, q8_0 variants). All packaged with a detached signature and SHA256 sums. The installation doc explictly lists post-install checks and an offline license activation step.
[01:58] Ravi Patel: When you say "offline license activation" — is that a license file we drop in /etc/redwood? Or a token exchange that requires a one-time trampoline online? What's the flow?
[02:12] Priya Shah: Good question. For air-gapped, we support two modes. Mode A: offline license file — we generate an activation package on our side tied to a host fingerprint you provide (MAC + machine-id + optional HSM cert), we sign it, you drop it into /etc/redwood/license.d/, service picks it up and validates local signature with our public key. No outbound at runtime. Mode B: one-time activation token — you do an ephemeral handshake where you take a CSR, we produce a signed license, you import it. Both are fully documented.
[02:46] Miguel Torres: We prefer Mode A. How do you tie the license to the machine? We can't have floating licenses that get copied across nodes.
[02:55] Priya Shah: It's a host bind: we use machine-id+primary NIC MAC address. For HSM setups we can bind to a cert's public key fingerprint instead, so you keep the key material inside the HSM.
[03:10] Dana Li: That sounds OK. We also need a reproducible checksum and a way to verify the signature offline — do you provide OpenSSL commands?
[03:18] Alex Nguyen: Yes, the install doc includes exact openssl commands for signature verification and a script we call verify-artifact.sh that does sha256sum and then checks the detached signature. We'll include example outputs in the doc so it's easy for auditors.
[03:36] Ravi Patel: Great. Now, drivers — we have heterogenous nodes; which CUDA/cuDNN/NCCL combinations should we aim for? We've had issues in the past where runtime fails due to mismatched cuDNN minor versions even though CUDA matched.
[03:52] Priya Shah: Right. Short version: Redwood runtime is compiled against CUDA 12.1 and cuDNN 9 in our current 2.1 release, but it's tolerant within certain ABI ranges. We maintain a compatibility matrix: CUDA 11.8+ (partial), 12.0 and 12.1 recommended. cuDNN 8.x has some incompat in corner cases, so we recommend 9.x for best perf. NCCL 2.18+ for multi-GPU. We'll share the matrix.
[04:18] Miguel Torres: We have some hosts stuck on RHEL7 with older drivers. Is there a lightweight fallback? We can't reimage everything before pilot.
[04:28] Priya Shah: There is a fallback path — a CPU-only shim and quantized int8 paths, but latency will be very different. For mixed fleets we recommend dedicating GPU-capable nodes to inference and letting older hosts do preprocessing. We can also provide container images with vendor-specific driver wrappers, but they still need kernel driver compatibility.
[04:50] Dana Li: In terms of install layout — will you provide RPM/deb packages or tarballs? Our offline install processes prefer distro packages for patching.
[04:59] Alex Nguyen: We can provide both. For air-gapped installs, we typically give authors an ISO image and rpm bundles. For Debian shops we provide .deb bundles. The tarball is the fallback. We'll include systemd unit files and a post-install verification playbook.
[05:18] Ravi Patel: Ok, let's talk KV cache persistence. If a node restarts, how do you warm the KV cache quickly so p95 latency doesn't spike?
[05:28] Priya Shah: Good, KV cache persist is something we observed in larger deployments. The runtime persists a compact snapshot of the KV cache to disk periodically (configurable). On restart it loads the snapshot and resumes. For truly cold starts, we support a pre-warm utility that replays recent prefixes from a snapshot or prebuilt warm-up trace. For air-gapped, we can deliver pre-warmed snapshots as part of the artifact if you can allocate scratch disk space on the nodes.
[05:56] Miguel Torres: How big are those snapshots typically? For a working set of a 50-concurrent chat users per node?
[06:08] Priya Shah: It depends on sequence length and model. As a rule of thumb, a small snapshot with common prefixes is tens to low hundreds of MBs per model. The full KV dump for very long contexts can be multiple GBs. We'll provide tooling to prune and limit snapshots to a size you want.
[06:26] Dana Li: Another security question — where are those snapshots encrypted? We need them encrypted at rest and you mentioned HSM earlier.
[06:34] Alex Nguyen: By default snapshots are encrypted with a node-local key managed by the Redwood agent. For air-gapped setups we recommend integrating with your KMS/HSM — the runtime supports wrapping keys with HSM and storing only wrapped keys on disk. We'll include a sample config that shows how to call PKCS#11 for a common HSM.
[06:54] Ravi Patel: On batching — what's your latency impact with continuous batching enabled? For our chat use case p50 target is 120ms, p95 320ms at 50 qps.
[07:06] Priya Shah: Continuous batching trades a small p50 increase for throughput. On A100 80GB we see per-request latency p50 around 90-130ms depending on sequence length with dynamic batching and concurrency 8-16. The key is shaping queue wait timers; you can set max_batch_delay_ms to 5-10ms to keep p50 low. For p95 you want smaller batch sizes or reserved lanes for tail-sensitive traffic. We'll provide recommended configs for your target.
[07:36] Miguel Torres: Do you recommend explicit reserved CPUs for the agent process? We saw issues where the agent contends with other system services and introduces jitter.
[07:45] Priya Shah: Yes, we recommend pinning the agent and runtime threads to dedicated CPU cores and using cgroup isolation. We include a sample systemd slice that pins cores and sets RLIMITS. That reduces jitter significantly.
[08:02] Dana Li: Quantization — you have a precompiled quant pack; how much accuracy drop do you see for q4_0 vs q8_0? We run a sensitive customer-facing assistant and can't have hallucination regressions.
[08:13] Priya Shah: Quantization quality varies by model. Our evaluations for common LLaMA-style models show q4_0 with well-tuned per-channel quant has negligible quality degradation on most prompting tasks; q8_0 preserves even more fidelity but gives less perf gains. For safety-critical prompts we recommend running Redwood Optimize evals against your prompt set — we can do a quick eval for a small representative set to quantify delta.
[08:42] Miguel Torres: Can the quant packs be loaded offline as well?
[08:47] Priya Shah: Yes, they are part of the runtime bundle — encrypted and signed. You can toggle per-model quant profile in the model config.
[08:56] Alex Nguyen: Quick operational note — we also ship a nightly check script that reports health to a local log; it doesn't call home. For enterprise installs we include an option to push logs to your local ELK/Graylog.
[09:12] Ravi Patel: Let's get into concrete driver versions — I'll read our exact inventory. We have: RHEL8 + NVIDIA driver 535.54.03 on A100-80GB, RHEL8 + driver 470 on some legacy V100s, and one node with CUDA 11.4 installed.
[09:34] Priya Shah: 535.x is fine — compatible with CUDA 12-ish stacks if the kernel driver is recent. The 470 stack for V100 is older; supported but you may need to run a slightly older runtime build or isolate V100s. We'll provide runtime-legacy package for 470/CUDA11.4. For the V100 nodes, performance will be substantially lower and certain kernel APIS used for fast attention may not be available.
[09:58] Miguel Torres: If we have a mix, can we route requests by capability? For example route high-latency tolerant batch workloads to V100s and strict-latency to A100s?
[10:07] Priya Shah: Yes, routing policy supports capability tags — we include a smart router that can route by model variant, GPU capability, or latency tier. In private deployments the control plane runs locally and you can set policies in the console or via the config file.
[10:24] Dana Li: About artifact transfer: we can accept signed ISO images via our secure courier (sneakernet). Do you provide checksums for mid-transfer integrity?
[10:33] Alex Nguyen: Yes — ISO + .sha256 + .asc signature. We recommend validating both checksum and signature post-transfer. We'll include a transfer checklist for auditors.
[10:46] Ravi Patel: Any gotchas with container runtimes? We use containerd 1.6 and runc; does Redwood runtime assume Docker?
[10:55] Priya Shah: We support containerd and Docker. The runtime packages a minimal OCI image and we provide an example ctr/containerd config. The only caveat we've seen is an old runc version that lacks certain io_uring optimizations — not critical but impacts perf.
[11:12] Miguel Torres: What about SELinux/AppArmor? We run strict policies.
[11:19] Priya Shah: We have an AppArmor profile and an SELinux module. The install script can optionally load them. If you run zones with strict MAC, we recommend test installs with permissive first and then switch to enforcing after confirming file contexts.
[11:35] Dana Li: For shipping RPMs, will you include GPG keys and instructions to verify?
[11:40] Alex Nguyen: Yup, GPG-signed RPMs + instructions. We'll also include a small offline repo layout if you want to host packages locally.
[11:50] Ravi Patel: Ok — performance smoke test plan? What should we run after install to confirm the node meets our SLOs?
[11:58] Priya Shah: We'll provide a smoke test script that runs fixed prompts at configurable concurrency and measures p50/p95/p99 latencies and throughput. We'll include sample prompts and an expected baseline for the model variant. For air-gapped, the script writes results to a JSON you can attach to the ticket.
[12:20] Miguel Torres: If we discover a driver mismatch post-install, can we swap the runtime binary quickly or do we need to reimage?
[12:30] Priya Shah: You can swap runtime packages without reimaging. We design the agent to be hot-swappable; you pull the new runtime package and restart the service. Kernel driver mismatches (NVIDIA kernel module vs user-space driver) are a different story and may require a reboot.
[12:44] Alex Nguyen: Quick sidebar — we've seen issues where the driver was updated but kernel module lagged behind; that causes CUDA initialization failures. We recommend updating user-space and kernel modules in the same maintenance window.
[12:58] Dana Li: About verification: can you provide a minimal set of openssl commands and a Jenkins pipeline example that runs offline? Our ops prefer pipeline-based verification when transferring artifacts.
[13:10] Priya Shah: Yes, sample Jenkinsfile is in the repo we'll send. It runs sha256sum, then gpg --verify. We also provide a small Go binary that validates the manifest and signature if you prefer a binary check.
[13:28] Miguel Torres: Any notes on licensing terms for the offline license? Does the license include automatic renewals or do we need to request new activations?
[13:36] Alex Nguyen: For pilots we issue time-limited offline licenses (30/90 days). For production we offer a signed license bundle tied to HSM with automated renewals if you open an ops channel with Redwood. Renewals are either pushed via secure courier or done via a one-time token exchange depending on your preference.
[13:54] Ravi Patel: Let's capture the exact files you will provide.
[13:58] Priya Shah: Sure — a short list: redwood-agent-2.1.tgz, runtime-image-2025.04.tar.gz, quant-pack-q4_q8.tar.gz (optional), pre-warm-kvcache-2025.snapshot.gz (optional), rpm-bundles/ and deb-bundles/, install-checklist.md, verify-artifact.sh, sample-jenkinsfile, GPG public key and .asc signatures, license-activation-tool and docs.
[14:30] Miguel Torres: Great. For the pre-warm snapshot — we need to know the footprint and memory requirements. Can you provide an estimate for our fleet?
[14:38] Priya Shah: We'll need your typical context lengths and concurrency per model. As a conservative default, assume 200MB per model for a small warm-up snapshot. We'll adapt after we see your traffic profile.
[14:52] Dana Li: Anything else on the runtime side — telemetry, logs, and retention?
[15:00] Alex Nguyen: By default nothing leaves your network. Logs are local; retention is configurable. If you want Redwood-hosted telemetry for dedicated customers, we can enable a pull model with explicit approval. But for air-gapped pilot, everything stays on-prem.
[15:15] Ravi Patel: Ok good. Can you also run a quick perf sim with quant q4_0 vs fp16 for one of our sample prompts?
[15:23] Priya Shah: Yes, that's part of the follow-up. Priya will run a small eval against three representative prompts and share a CSV with p50/p95/throughput numbers.
[15:33] Miguel Torres: One last operational ask — do you support rolling upgrades of runtime with zero downtime? We need a canary path.
[15:42] Priya Shah: We do. The runtime supports side-by-side package installs and we have a built-in canary flag to shift 5-10% traffic before full rollout. For private deployments the control-plane has a rollout API that coordinates draining and bringing nodes back.
[15:56] Dana Li: Perfect. Anything we missed?
[16:00] Alex Nguyen: I think that's most of it. Recap of deliverables and timeline: Alex packages artifacts + checksums by 24th. Priya runs the driver matrix and perf evals by 26th. Miguel confirms transfer method and provides inventory by 25th. Follow-up call 29th to review smoke test and pilot kickoff.
[16:18] Miguel Torres: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[16:21] Ravi Patel: Thanks.
[16:23] Dana Li: Thanks.
[16:25] Alex Nguyen: We'll send the S3 link for the private artifact bucket (note: link is for reference in doc; for air-gapped we will prepare ISO and signed packages).
